title: 15 Sales closing questions to close deals — data from 2,000+ calls
summary: Looking for sales closing questions to close more deals? Here are the best closing questions we’ve found from analyzing our own sales calls.
body_markdown:
Picture this: you get an incoming call from a new lead. You understand what they’re looking for and give them your pitch.


They don’t respond. An awkward silence sets in. Then you ask the only question you can think of: *“Are you ready to buy?”* They promptly hang up.


What you need are sales closing questions.


Sales closing questions are prompts designed to guide a prospect toward a decision, whether that’s booking another meeting, signing up for a free trial, or saying yes to the deal.


They help you understand where the prospect stands and what needs to happen next to keep things moving. Whether you’re navigating a tricky pricing objection or trying to keep momentum with a slow-moving lead, the right question can mean the difference between a deal won and a deal lost.


We collected data from over 2,000 calls from our[own sales team](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-our-sales-team-uses-quo/) to find the most effective closing questions you can use. We also provide the best closing techniques and tips to help you consistently move deals forward.


##


Why do sales closing questions matter?


Sales closing questions are tools to help you connect more deeply with your leads in your calls. Here’s how:


- **Build rapport.** Closing questions help you establish a dialogue with your prospects, especially in the initial[discovery call](https://www.quo.com/blog/discovery-call/) . Launching into your pitch can feel transactional and may not speak to your prospects. The right closing questions can help you build trust with your leads, which can make a real difference.
- **Uncover prospect pain points.** Understand what prospects want and how you can meet their specific needs. Every customer is different, and you can’t use the same sales strategy in every situation. Closing questions help you tailor your sales approach in an authentic manner.
- **Get the prospect to name their objections.** Build a comfortable, open dialogue where you can address their concerns head-on — because nobody has time for mind-reading games. Once you identify objections, you can use your objection-handling scripts to resolve them.
- **Set clear next steps.** The best sales calls end with an action plan and timeline, not just a vague *“We’ll think about it.”* Closing questions help you pin down a date and time for your next steps.


##


11 Top sales closing techniques with examples


If you’re stuck between “maybe” and “not right now,” these sales strategy techniques help you lead the conversation without pushing too hard:


### 1. The next step and scheduling close


**What it is:** You ask to book the job or service, the estimate visit, or the follow-up call before you hang up.


**Why it works:** A date on the calendar keeps the customer from calling the next business on their list.


**Example:** *I have Thursday morning or Friday afternoon open. Which works better for you?*


### 2. The hesitation check close


**What it is:** You ask what’s still holding the customer back before you ask for the job. You can then handle any objections they share.


**Why it matters:** You can address a concern about price, timing, or trust while they’re still on the phone, instead of finding out a week later when they stop replying.


**Example:** *Is anything making you hesitate about moving forward?*


### 3. The relevance check close


**What it is:** After you explain part of your service, you ask whether it solves the problem they called about.


**Why it matters:** It connects what you offer to their situation one piece at a time, so you know what matters to them before you give a quote.


**Example:** *Would that take care of the issue you mentioned?*


### 4. The fit validation close


**What it is:** You check that the customer understands and likes what you’ve walked them through so far.


**Why it matters:** It keeps the call a conversation instead of a sales pitch and tells you where they stand before you talk price.


**Example:** *What are your thoughts so far?*


### 5. The timeline and urgency close


**What it is:** You ask when the customer needs this done or how pressing the problem is.


**Why it matters:** It helps you[qualify leads](https://www.quo.com/blog/lead-qualification/) by separating a customer ready to book from one collecting quotes. Someone with a leaking pipe or wanting a lease starting Monday is buying. Someone who says “just seeing what’s out there” is comparing.


**Example:** *When are you hoping to get this done?*


### 6. The decision-maker loop close


**What it is:** You ask whether anyone else, like a spouse, business partner, or landlord, needs to sign off.


**Why it matters:** Learning about a second decision-maker after you’ve sent the quote is how jobs go quiet. Ask early so you can include them or schedule a time when they’re available. It’s the authority check in the[BANT framework](https://www.quo.com/blog/bant-sales/) .


**Example:** *Is there anyone else who’ll want to weigh in before you decide?*


### 7. The comparison close


**What it is:** You ask how your offer compares to their current provider or other quotes they’ve gotten.


**Why it matters:** When someone already has a provider or a competing quote, it gets them to talk about where you come out ahead and shows you what you’re up against.


**Example:** *How does this compare to what you’re using now or other quotes you’ve gotten?*


### 8. The summary close


**What it is:** You recap what the customer told you they need and how you’ll deliver it, then ask for the go-ahead.


**Why it matters:** It shows you listened, puts the whole picture in one place, and makes saying yes feel like the logical next step.


**Example:** *So, you need the AC serviced before the heat wave, you want someone to come this week, and you’d like a maintenance plan so this doesn’t happen again. Do I have that right?*


### 9. The open-floor sweep close


**What it is:** You invite remaining questions before moving on or wrapping up.


**Why it matters:** It works as a check-in partway through the call but barely works at the end. The same question gets a real answer mid-conversation and a quick “nope, I’m good” in the last minute of a call.


**Example:** *What questions do you have that we haven’t covered?*


### 10. The deadline close


**What it is:** You give the customer a reason to book by a certain date, often tied to a discount, open slot, or seasonal rate.


**Why it matters:** It gives them a reason to act now instead of “thinking about it” and calling someone else.


**Example:** *If you book by Friday, I can lock in this price and get you on the schedule next week.*


**Note:** Use this close sparingly and only for prospects and deals where it matters. If every customer gets a deal, they’ll learn to wait for one.


### 11. The trial close


**What it is:** You offer a low-commitment first step, like a single visit, a free estimate, a consultation, or a trial period, before a bigger commitment.


**Why it matters:** It lowers the risk of saying yes. The customer gets to see your work firsthand before signing up for the full job or an ongoing plan.


**Example:** *Why don’t we start with one cleaning? If you like the results, we can set up the monthly plan.*


##


15 sales closing questions that actually work


Now that you have several techniques under your belt, let’s look at 15 sales closing questions that help you build rapport, uncover potential objections, and get closer to a “yes.”


### 1. How are you feeling about this so far?


This open-ended question invites honesty, builds trust, and helps set expectations. It shows you care about how the experience is landing. It also gives potential customers a chance to raise concerns they haven’t voiced yet.


### 2. Does this align with your team’s needs?


Encourage prospects to evaluate your solution through their company’s priorities. You’re also asking them to “connect the dots” out loud, which is a subtle yet powerful form of buy-in.


Your goal with this question is to make sure that you’re highlighting all the features of your solution, that it’s a fit for them, and that you’re not missing anything important.


### 3. How does this compare with your current solution or others you’ve evaluated?


Find out how you stack up: what they like and dislike compared to other options on the market.


You might also uncover hidden objections, preferences, or internal benchmarks that haven’t come up yet.


### 4. Is there anything you want to see that we haven’t covered yet?


This question shows that you’re collaborative and thorough, not rushing the closing conversation or looking past the prospect’s needs. It also helps prevent last-minute surprises that could delay the decision-making process.


### 5. If this feels like a good fit, the next step is usually \[product demo/trial/quote\]. Does \[x date\] work for you?


An example of the next step and scheduling close, this question invites agreement without pressure.


It works especially well when the prospect seems engaged but hasn’t explicitly agreed to move forward yet.


### 6. Is there anyone else you’d want to bring into this conversation before deciding?


This question is another example of the decision-maker close. If you’re selling to another company, this could be a manager or a senior leader. If you’re talking to an individual, it could be a family member or a legal representative.


### 7. Would you prefer \[option A\] or \[option B\]?


Giving potential clients two strong next steps makes it easier for them to move forward. You’re giving them a sense of control and ownership while still guiding the close.


### 8. If budget weren’t a concern, is this the right solution?


By separating value from cost, you can better understand what’s really blocking a sales deal.


If they say yes, it’s a pricing conversation, not a product one. If they say no, you can address any customer needs or issues you haven’t been able to address so far.


### 9. What do integrations look like for you?


This question shows you’re trying to understand what other tools they use, what data needs to sync, and whether they expect automation out of the box. It also signals that you’re thinking about long-term fit and ease of use, not just making the sale.


If integrations are a dealbreaker, it’s better to find out early. And if your solution fits seamlessly, this gives you a chance to highlight that.


### 10. What would stop you from moving forward today?


This is another example of the hesitation check close. It opens the conversation to cover any items that haven’t been discussed yet.


### 11. When would you ideally want to have this rolled out?


This is another version of the timeline check close. This question helps frame urgency around *their* internal timeframe, not yours. It also gives you something concrete to work from when navigating next steps like follow-ups and proposals.


### 12. Just to confirm — is \[pain point\] still your team’s biggest priority?


Revisiting the initial pain point shows you’ve been listening. It also gives the prospect a chance to reaffirm their sense of urgency or update you if something’s changed on their end.


### 13. Would that be beneficial to you?


Here’s a simple, yet effective, relevance check question you can use in the early phases of a conversation with your customers. Once you understand what they’re looking for and present some options where you can serve them, use this question to test their interest.


If they answer positively, you can continue with your pitch. If they answer negatively, you can change course to dig deeper into what they might be looking for.


### 14. Would it be easier to decide if you could try it with your team first?


This question is a version of the trial close for your customers. Some products and services have more value when a team uses them instead of individuals. For example, a shared phone system that lets teams handle incoming calls and texts together — sound familiar?


### 15. If we could make the pricing work, could you commit by \[date\]?


This question is another version of the deadline close. They may have questions or requirements about their pricing estimate. Asking this question can address that concern and give them confidence it will be handled. It also gives both of you a clear timeline on implementation or service delivery.

##


Actionable tips for closing more deals


Here’s how to turn strong sales conversations into actual closes — and set yourself up to do it consistently.


### Use transition statements to guide the conversation


Try using transition phrases like *“Usually at this point…”* or *“The next step for most teams is…”*


These work because they make closing feel like a natural next step in your discovery call. Instead of stumbling through *“So… are you interested?”* you can confidently guide the conversation forward.


### Keep your follow-ups short, helpful, and action-oriented


Send a recap within 24 hours that covers what you discussed, any concerns they raised, and one clear next step.


Use[Quo Agent](https://www.quo.com/product/quo-agent) to draft your follow-ups in seconds. It uses the context of your past calls and text threads to draft the perfect reply. Here’s a[follow-up text example](https://www.quo.com/blog/follow-up-text-examples/) prompt you can use:


*Draft follow-up messages for any contacts I spoke to in the last 24 hours. Include what we discussed, any concerns they raised, and one clear next step. Keep it concise and friendly.*


These can save you hours of writing time each week.


### Frame urgency around their goals


Tie urgency to their business timeline to make it helpful. Find out when they want to launch or implement your solution, then work backward. For example, if they want a kitchen renovation done before the next school year starts, you can say, *“To hit your timeline, we should get started with blueprints and designs by mid-May.”*


### Use social proof to make the product’s value feel tangible


Share a quick story about a customer who had the same problem, and include specific results when possible.


Try something like: *“We worked with another agency that was missing leads after hours. After setting up our system, they captured 40% more qualified prospects in their first month.”*


You can also cite customer testimonials from your website if you want to get more specific.


### Use open-ended questions during discovery


Closing questions are typically associated with the end of a deal, right before customers are ready to buy a product or service. But every step of a sales conversation has its own closing step to guide prospects through the sales process.


Open-ended closing questions help leads open up about their situation and what they’re looking for. They encourage prospects to share more context instead of directly answering a straightforward question.


Here are a few examples of open-ended questions you can use in your discovery calls:


**After presenting your pitch:** *From what you’ve seen or heard, what would be the most helpful for you?*


**Before scheduling the next step:** *What else would you want to know before we book the next step?*


You can also use open-ended questions as micro-closes throughout the conversation to keep prospects engaged. For example, *“What are your thoughts so far?”*


**Pro tip:**[Sales AI tools](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-ai/) like Quo can help you track which customer stories lead to successful closes. You can then use those examples in future conversations to increase your closing rate.


##


Open-ended vs closed-ended closing questions


When you’re building your sales scripts, you might be tempted to use open-ended questions to encourage conversation. Our sales calls show it’s more nuanced. The type of question matters less than whether it’s a substantive question. Plus, where you ask a closing question matters to the quality of your conversations. Here’s a comparison of these two types of questions:


### What our sales calls show


We evaluated whether our team used more open-ended or closed-ended questions. We found that they leaned more heavily on closed-ended questions about 70% of the time.


That isn’t a problem on its own. Substantive closed questions, like asking about hesitations or timelines, get answers as long and detailed as open ones.


Our team tends to ask open-ended questions earlier in calls to encourage prospects to share objections as they arise. During walkthroughs, they use micro-close questions so they can address concerns in real time instead of pushing them to the end of the call.


**The takeaway:** Don’t shy away from asking closed-ended questions, especially when you want to confirm details with your prospects.


### When to use open vs closed-ended questions


The best sales reps use both open-ended and closed-ended questions.


Open-ended questions Closed-ended questions


Use them for Understanding priorities


Surfacing hidden objections


Mapping the decision path


Checking reactions after a walkthrough or quote Confirming details


Locking in a date or next step


Checking agreement before moving on


Asking for a decision


How they start What, How, Why, Tell me about, Describe, Walk me through Is, Are, Do, Did, Would, Will, Could, Can, Was, Were, Have, Has


Examples “Where does getting this fixed fall on your list right now?”


“What’s making you hesitate about going ahead?”


“What do the next steps look like on your end?”


“What are your thoughts on the quote so far?” “So, it’s the two upstairs bathrooms. Does that sound right?”


“Can I provide the estimate to you on Friday morning? Would that work?”


“Does that plan make sense to you?”


“Are you ready for me to put you on the schedule?”


### How to make your closing questions stronger


Sometimes, you may find that you’re using the wrong type of question in your conversation. Here are a few ways you can tweak these questions and make them stronger:


#### Change your questions to get longer replies


Closed-ended questions are direct and tend to get “yes/no” answers from leads. Open-ended questions give your prospects room to share longer answers. You can use the word choices shared above to restructure your questions:


- *“Any other questions?”* → *“What have we missed so far?”* **
The open version draws longer, more specific answers.


- *“Do you want to schedule a follow-up?” → “What would be the ideal next step for you?”* ** ** The closed version gets a yes and a date. The open version tells you who they need to talk to and when they’ll decide.


- *“Do you have a timeline in mind?” → “What does your timeline look like?”* ** ** Both provide answers, but the open version rarely gets a one-word reply.


#### Turn generic questions into specific ones


At times, you may need to turn an open-ended question into a closed-ended one. One reason is that open-ended questions can feel generic, so prospects don’t answer them directly. A question tied to what the customer just told you or to a specific next step, is harder to ignore. Here are a few examples:


- **Generic:** “Want to set up another time to talk?”


- **Specific:** “Would it help if I came by Saturday when your husband’s home, so you can both see the layout before deciding?”


- **Generic:** “Any other questions?”
- **Specific:** “You mentioned the last company left a mess. Is there anything about how we clean up after a job that you want to know?”
- **Generic:** “Do you have a timeline in mind?”


- **Specific:** “Your tenants move in on the 1st. Do you want the unit painted before then, or is the first week okay?”


##


Common mistakes that kill deals


Even the best sales reps can sabotage their close by falling into traps like:


- **Being overly aggressive with assumptive language.** Pushing too hard with *“So we’re all set to move forward?”* can turn off cautious buyers. Use confident but flexible phrasing like *“If this feels like a good fit, the next step is usually \[X\]. Would that work for you?”*
- **Ignoring red flags or objections.** When a prospect hesitates or mentions a concern, don’t move ahead with your pitch. Listen to what’s bothering them and address it directly before moving forward.
- **Using pushy sales phrases.** Saying *“You should definitely do this”* or *“Trust me, this will work”* makes prospects feel like you’re trying to pressure them into buying. Use softer language like *“Many clients find this helpful”* or *“Here’s what typically works well”* instead.
- **Failing to follow up with clear next steps.** So many calls lose momentum because there’s no recap or follow-up. Use tools like Quo’s scheduled messages or[text message templates](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-text-message-examples/) to follow up quickly and stay top of mind.
- **Not using call recordings and summaries to hand off context.** When customers move to another team member, they shouldn’t have to repeat their whole story. Share[call recordings](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-call-recordings/) and detailed[summaries](https://www.quo.com/features/call-summary) to make handoffs smooth, and use[sales collaboration](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-collaboration/) tools to keep everyone in the loop.

##


FAQs


**What are sales closing questions?**


Sales closing questions are questions you ask to move a customer toward a decision, like booking the job, scheduling an estimate, or agreeing to a next step. They also tell you where the customer stands and what’s still holding them back.


**What are the top five sales closing techniques?**


The top sales closing techniques can vary by business type. Here are the ones applicable for most businesses:
1. **Next step and scheduling close.** Book the job or follow up before you hang up.
**2. Hesitation check close.** Ask what’s still holding them back while you can still address it.
**3. Timeline and urgency close.** Find out when they need it done to tell a serious buyer from a browser.
**4. Summary close.** Recap what they need and how you’ll deliver it, then ask for the go-ahead.
**5. Trial close.** Offer a low-commitment first step, like a single visit or free estimate.


**What is a sales closing strategy?**


A sales closing strategy is your plan for turning an interested customer into a booked job. It means choosing which closing questions to ask and when, based on where the customer is in the conversation. A good strategy qualifies the customer early, checks for hesitation before you give a price, and always ends the call with a specific next step on the calendar, so the deal doesn’t depend on them calling you back.
